Citations are recorded as written in the OCR text, and statuses note when a defect may be an OCR artifact rather than an error in the original.

W.R. Grace and Misco attachments are Justia web prints (one PDF page of opinion text each, plus navigation pages); locations use the embedded 'Page 461 U.S. ...'/'Page 484 U.S. ...' markers. Justia artifacts were compared with the official texts on CourtListener: Misco p.42 'W. R. Grace ..., 461 U. S. 757, 334 U. S. 766', Misco n.10 '415 F.2d 186', Misco p.35 '(CA5 1986)', Grace p.765 page-marker garble ('4 and S. 765') and n.1 'W. P. Grace' (record cite, not counted).
FOP v. PERB attachment is a FindLaw web print (14 PDF pages, pages 8-14 are site boilerplate with no opinion text); compared against the official opinion text on CourtListener.

D.C. Code attachment is a 2026 web print of the official code site; navigation links (§§ 1-605.01, 1-605.03) and site publication metadata (Law 26-140, Act 26-357, Public Law 115-334) were not counted as citations.

DCMR attachment is the D.C. Department of Human Resources' DPM Chapter 16 page (Transmittal 238), not a DCMR print, and reproduces all of Chapter 16. Only citations to authority outside Chapter 16 and the D.C. Register addendum were itemized; Chapter 16's internal cross-references to its own sections (for example '§ 1618', '§§ 1626 through 1637') and the DPM 'Active Issuances' list were not itemized.

Record citations inside the real opinions (App., briefs, record pages, 'ante'/'supra note' cross-references within the same opinion) were not counted. Name-only references to the same statute after a full citation in the same paragraph (e.g. later bare 'CMPA', 'Title VII', 'Back Pay Act') were counted once per document.

Prompts were counted from each assignment's own prompt text (input.json 'prompt'); instruction.md for assignments 2-5 repeats earlier prompts and those repetitions were not counted again. Rubric fields were counted per criterion: authorities named in the criterion text and each authority in the source field. Justification fields quote the prompt and add no authority of their own; those quotations were not counted again.

The two scenario memoranda (comparator_discipline_cases.pdf; supplemental_comparator_disclosure.pdf) are record evidence; their citation in rubric source fields was not counted. Fictional-by-design records are the scenario adjudications (Final Notice, Award, PERB Opinion No. 1904) and scenario disciplinary case numbers.

Coverage of embedded citations is a census, not full verification: of the citations inside the five real opinions and the regulation, those marked UNABLE_TO_VERIFY were resolved for existence only (CourtListener citation lookup or the citator links in the official opinion text) or not retrieved at all (legislative history, Federal Register, executive orders, Comptroller General decisions, unpublished Civil Service Commission and early MSPB decisions, the Federal Personnel Manual, treatises and law reviews, 1980 versions of Title 5). Their pin cites and propositions were not read.

No purchased databases were used. Primary sources read: CourtListener opinion texts; code.dccouncil.gov (official D.C. Code); dcregs.dc.gov (official DCMR section documents); go.mpdconline.com (MPD General Order PER-120.21, eff. Nov. 27, 2022); Cornell LII for 5 U.S.C. § 5596. The MPD-FOP collective bargaining agreement and the PERB Dexter Allen decision were not retrieved.

A supplemental GPT-6 Sol primary-source pass attempted 124 previously unverified occurrences: 69 verified, one minor defect, 54 still unable to verify. Its per-reference attempts and remaining access limits are retained; the original unattempted status is historical, not the current result.

A further GPT-6 Sol primary-source pass attempted all 64 unverified citations added by the second census: 63 statutory referents and supporting premises verified, one October 2019 D.C. Register notice still unavailable. The 63 earlier unattempted judgments are retained only as history.

citations.cited_for: MPD's arguments that the Award is contrary to law

first_check.explanation: Section 1-605.02(6) permits PERB to set aside an award 'on its face ... contrary to law and public policy' (conjunctive). Framing separate 'contrary-to-law' and 'public-policy' exceptions departs from the statutory wording, although the D.C. Court of Appeals itself discusses the 'contrary to ... public policy' limitation separately (MPD v. PERB, 901 A.2d at 789) and in FOP (973 A.2d at 179) declined to decide the conjunctive argument. The provision also governs PERB's review of arbitration awards; court review of PERB orders runs through § 1-617.13.
first_check.excerpt_read: § 1-605.02(6): "the award on its face is contrary to law and public policy"; FOP, 973 A.2d at 179: "FOP further contends that the CMPA authorizes PERB to reverse an arbitral award only if the award is contrary to both 'law and public policy' ... By raising this argument for the first time in its brief to this court".

second_check.explanation: The statutory text uses the conjunction “law and public policy” and defines PERB award-review authority. FOP permits a reasonable PERB construction and did not decide whether both prongs must be met because that objection was waived. The phrasing as separate exceptions is imprecise, but should not be treated as a decisive legal error without the case-law qualification.
second_check.excerpt_read: §1-605.02(6): award “on its face is contrary to law and public policy”; FOP, 973 A.2d at 179: conjunctive argument not preserved.

citations.context: required 2 points

first_check.explanation: Section 1-605.02(6) permits PERB to set aside an award 'on its face ... contrary to law and public policy' (conjunctive). Framing separate 'contrary-to-law' and 'public-policy' exceptions departs from the statutory wording, although the D.C. Court of Appeals itself discusses the 'contrary to ... public policy' limitation separately (MPD v. PERB, 901 A.2d at 789) and in FOP (973 A.2d at 179) declined to decide the conjunctive argument. The provision also governs PERB's review of arbitration awards; court review of PERB orders runs through § 1-617.13.
first_check.excerpt_read: § 1-605.02(6): "the award on its face is contrary to law and public policy"; FOP, 973 A.2d at 179: "FOP further contends that the CMPA authorizes PERB to reverse an arbitral award only if the award is contrary to both 'law and public policy' ... By raising this argument for the first time in its brief to this court".

second_check.explanation: The statutory text uses the conjunction “law and public policy” and defines PERB award-review authority. FOP permits a reasonable PERB construction and did not decide whether both prongs must be met because that objection was waived. The phrasing as separate exceptions is imprecise, but should not be treated as a decisive legal error without the case-law qualification.
second_check.excerpt_read: §1-605.02(6): award “on its face is contrary to law and public policy”; FOP, 973 A.2d at 179: conjunctive argument not preserved.

The 1978 enacted text was read for most Douglas title 5 citations; the separately printed 1980 U.S.C.A. edition was not collated.

The accessible appellate opinion reproductions generally omit reporter page-break markers, so quoted propositions were checked in opinion context while some exact printed pins cannot be confirmed from that transcription.

CourtListener citation search exposed metadata and limited snippets, but direct opinion-text endpoints were inaccessible without authentication or returned access errors; no credentials were requested.

Older Civil Service Commission decisions/manuals, specified congressional reports and hearings, some Court of Claims and district-court opinions, and copyrighted secondary texts did not yield readable cited passages after the recorded access attempts.
This is the first substantive source-reading check for these refs. Any newly flagged problem requires a separate independent second check before integration.
